3119537.twitter_share_message: “Similar structure to the ‘Cousin Stephen, you will never….’ paragraph. There is a triangulation …” —@Genius

children: Similar structure to the ‘Cousin Stephen, you will never….’ paragraph. There is a triangulation between the introductory negative thought phrase in both paragraphs, the pause (‘Isle of saints’ and ‘I was young’) and some lighter phrases later on (‘o si, cierto!’ and ‘Ay, very like a whale’).

The triangulation is an effective delivery mechanism to sustain Joyce’s challenge in the stream of consciousness : maintain the apparently random flow of thoughts, break-up the self criticism so Stephen doesn’t appear a maudlin git and develop enough interest in the reader whilst Joyce skims the surface of Stephen’s experiences.
The next sentence skims his narcissistic episode in front of a mirror in Portrait of the Artist.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Le Tutu refers to the book by Leon Genonceaux, a similar proto modernist novel as Ulysses and deemed indecent. It has recently been published in English. The tattered, presumably by overuse, copies of the “ White Pants and red Knickers” may refer to a pornographic publication, possibly an invention by Joyce. Accompanied by the blue telegram ,distinctively French and bearing the news of Stephen’s dying mother, they are the travel mementos from Paris; suitably blue, white and red. Curiosity to show, an indication that the contents of the telegram are far less interesting to Stephen  then the exotic erotic.

range.content: He halted. I have passed the way to aunt Sara's. Am I not going there? Seems not. No-one about. He turned northeast and crossed the firmer sand towards the

4670894.twitter_share_message: “In plot terms, Stephen is going to the National Library to deliver a letter for Deasy but mainly…” —@Genius

children: In plot terms, Stephen is going to the National Library to deliver a letter for Deasy but mainly to deliver his theory on Hamlet to some literary figures. However Stephen doesn’t think about it at all in this chapter. Something else is going on. He has just left the Tower and said to himself that he won’t go back. He is at the time homeless. In this paragraph he indicates that he won’t go to his family (aunt Sara’s). The opportunity to go there leads to confused if not dark thoughts –
maze of cunning nets, human shells, dreadful thirst, midden, man’s ashes

In this paragraph he also shifts from this unsettling part of his life to ‘the firmer sand towards the Pigeon house’. This shift instigates thoughts/memories grounded in his experiences in Paris in which there are some home truths for Stephen but none of the dark words of the preceding paragraphs.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: I would also add that the dissociation between Stephen’s mind and feet “Am I not going there? Seems not” mirrors the alienation he felt of his lower body described earlier in this chapter.

5110169.twitter_share_message: “According to the Hindus, Mahamanvantara (Sanskrit) [from maha great + manvantara period of manif…” —@Genius

children: According to the Hindus, Mahamanvantara (Sanskrit) [from maha great + manvantara period of manifestation] is a great cycle of cosmic manifestation and activity, whether of a universe, solar system, or planet. Joyce frequently makes reference to Hindu esoteric words, texts and concepts. The mahamanvantara of a solar system also known as the Life of Brahma, is a period of 311,040,000,000,000 terrestrial years. A mahamanvantara of the earth-chain is a Day of Brahma or a period of seven rounds of the planetary chain. The day after the mahamanvantara is termed the Day-Be-With-Us a similar notion to the Christian Day of Judgment. At this point it is said all individualities are merged into one, each still possessing essential or intrinsic knowledge of itself. Hindus also state that at that time, what to us now is non-conscious or the unconscious, will be absolute consciousness.

5110193.twitter_share_message: “Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–94) is one the best known philosophers of the Renaissance er…” —@Genius

children: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–94) is one the best known philosophers of the Renaissance era. Pico was known for his remarkably original, idiosyncratic thought. In fact so esoteric and abstruse were his ideas that they were little studied until many years after they were published. Perhaps Joyce is implying here that his own work, due to its cryptic character might remain somehow obscured until read many, many years later and perhaps like the works of Pico they would still be highly relevant due to dealing with fundamental questions about human existence, life and death. Like Joyce’s, Pico’s work was highly concerned with the spiritual, with the notion of man as a sentient being. Pico believed that men, unlike beasts could change themselves through exercise of free will. Pico believed that when man philosophizes, he ascends the chain of being towards the angels, and communion with God. When he fails to exercise his intellect, he vegetates.
